items.topic: SQLite schema design: single DB vs per-brand DB
items.context: Brand Manager needs to store brands, assignments, assets metadata, and version history. A single SQLite database keeps things simple and queryable (e.g., 'show all brands assigned to scenario X'). Per-brand databases would isolate data but make cross-brand queries harder and complicate backup. Given the storage-steer pattern of scenario-isolated databases, a single DB at ~/.vrooli/brand-manager/brand-manager.db is the natural fit. Recommending option A.

options.label: Single SQLite database with tables: brands, brand_versions, assignments, assets
options.rationale: Simple, queryable, follows storage-steer conventions. One file to back up. Supports all needed queries natively.

options.label: Per-brand SQLite databases (one .db file per brand)
options.rationale: Maximum isolation, easy to export/share a single brand. But cross-brand queries require opening multiple DBs, and assignment tracking becomes awkward.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.topic: Design language file: format and generation ownership
items.context: You described a design language file in scenario docs that serves as agent context. Key questions: (1) Where exactly does it live? (2) What format? (3) Who generates/updates it — Brand Manager writes it during 'apply', or the user maintains it manually? Recommending option A — Brand Manager generates it during apply so it stays in sync with the structured brand data.

options.label: Brand Manager generates docs/DESIGN_LANGUAGE.md during 'apply' from brand data + user notes
options.rationale: Stays in sync with brand. Brand Manager can regenerate it when brand is updated. LLM-generated prose from structured data + user's freeform notes.

options.label: User creates/maintains docs/DESIGN_LANGUAGE.md manually; Brand Manager reads it during discovery but never writes it
options.rationale: Maximum user control. But risks going stale if brand changes.

options.label: Brand Manager generates a draft during 'apply', user can edit afterward; Brand Manager merges on re-apply
options.rationale: Best of both — auto-generated base with user customization. More complex merge logic needed.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.topic: Branding validation: marker convention for detecting applied themes
items.context: You described wanting a standard that's extensible across frameworks and languages. The scanner needs to reliably detect whether branding has been applied. Options range from file-convention-based (known paths) to marker-based (special comments/annotations in code). Recommending option A — a dedicated brand manifest file that Brand Manager writes on apply, which the scanner checks. This is the most reliable and framework-agnostic approach.

options.label: Brand manifest file: Brand Manager writes a .brand-manifest.json in the scenario root during apply, listing what was applied and where. Scanner checks this file against actual filesystem.
options.rationale: Most reliable — Brand Manager controls the manifest, scanner verifies reality matches it. Framework-agnostic. Easy to extend.

options.label: Marker comments in source files (e.g., /* @brand-manager: primary-color */ in CSS). Scanner greps for these markers.
options.rationale: Inline evidence in actual code. But fragile — markers can be accidentally deleted, and every framework needs different comment syntax.

options.label: Known file paths only (e.g., must have public/favicon.ico, src/theme/brand.css). No markers needed.
options.rationale: Simplest to implement. But can't verify correctness of content, only existence. A favicon could be a default placeholder.

options.label: Combination: manifest file for tracking + content hashing to verify files match expected brand assets
options.rationale: Most thorough — knows what was applied AND verifies it hasn't drifted. More complex but prevents silent brand rot.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.freeform: In-line evidence in actual code is the way to go because then it’s ground truth against what the code is actually doing. if we had a new config file for example that could drift from the actual code implementation so we’ll we do is define a a few supportive approaches and hope that the app can handle those and if not then we just simply don’t support automatic validation in those situations. I’m physically the idea is that overtime will come up with better standards and better ways to validate a certain branding decisions. And also, for some things will probably include checking multiple places for validation, and this might lead those properties to result in a partial validated status. For example, branding might require specific CSS or other styling set ups in addition to defining those in the manifest.json files. Just an example

items.context: The API needs to serve brands, assignments, assets, and validation status. The question is how to structure the REST endpoints. Recommending option A — resource-centric REST following the LPBS pattern (flat Go package, handler factory, gorilla/mux).

options.label: Resource-centric REST: /api/v1/brands, /api/v1/brands/{id}/versions, /api/v1/assignments, /api/v1/assets/{id}, /api/v1/scenarios/{name}/status, /api/v1/standards (for auditor)
options.rationale: Clean REST semantics. Each resource is independently addressable. Standards endpoint follows existing auditor provider pattern.

options.label: Scenario-centric REST: /api/v1/scenarios/{name}/brand, /api/v1/scenarios/{name}/apply, /api/v1/scenarios/{name}/validate
options.rationale: Scenario is the primary navigation axis. Simpler for agents that think in terms of 'brand this scenario'. But brands that span multiple scenarios are awkward.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.topic: Implementation phasing: build order within full-spec v1
items.context: Even though the MVP is full spec, we need a build order. The natural dependency chain: storage → API → CLI → discovery → generation → application → validation → UI. But some pieces can be parallelized. Recommending option A — foundation-first with validation early, since Scenario Auditor integration provides immediate ecosystem value even before generation is complete.

options.label: Phase 1: SQLite schema + storage + CRUD API + CLI basics. Phase 2: Discovery + validation (Scenario Auditor provider). Phase 3: Generation (OpenRouter). Phase 4: Application (programmatic + agent-assisted). Phase 5: UI wizard.
options.rationale: Validation early means branding gaps become visible across all scenarios quickly, creating pull for the generation/application features. Each phase is independently testable.

options.label: Phase 1: Full backend (storage + API + all business logic). Phase 2: CLI. Phase 3: UI.
options.rationale: Simpler phasing by surface. But delays validation feedback until everything is done.

options.label: Phase 1: End-to-end for a single brand element (e.g., just logos). Phase 2: Expand to colors. Phase 3: Typography. Phase 4: Full brand.
options.rationale: Vertical slices — each phase delivers a complete workflow for one brand element. Good for iterating UX. But lots of rework as each element has different generation/application patterns.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.topic: Opt-out mechanism: how test-only scenarios skip branding requirements
items.context: The spec says opt-out is via 'a tag or field in service.json'. This is one of the few places where Brand Manager needs to touch the service.json schema. Recommending option A — a simple boolean field, since it's the minimal schema change and makes Scenario Auditor checks trivial.

options.label: Add branding.opt_out: true to service.json schema. Scenario Auditor skips branding rules when this is set.
options.rationale: Minimal schema change. Self-documenting in the scenario's own config. Easy for auditor to check without querying Brand Manager.

options.label: Use existing tags field in service.json (e.g., tags: ['no-branding']). No schema change needed.
options.rationale: Zero schema change. But tags are freeform strings — typos silently fail, and there's no validation.

options.label: Brand Manager tracks opt-outs internally by scenario name. No service.json changes.
options.rationale: Keeps service.json clean. But requires Brand Manager to be running for auditor to know about opt-outs.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.text: The storage-steer skill confirms that Brand Manager should declare SQLite in service.json with schema: 'brand-manager', store data at ~/.vrooli/brand-manager/, and use initialization/storage/ for schema files. Asset files should use the api-core/storage module for filesystem operations with atomic writes.

Existing Scenario Auditor external providers (test-genie, tidiness-manager) all follow the same pattern: Go file in scenario-auditor/api/ named external_rules_<provider>.go, implementing externalRuleProvider interface, registered in init(). Brand Manager will need a similar file. The provider makes HTTP calls to Brand Manager's /api/v1/standards endpoint with a configurable timeout.
